title: Introduction
text: portop shows every TCP and UDP socket on a machine together with the process, service and container behind it and who can reach it, and lets you inspect or stop the owner. It runs on Linux, macOS and Windows, in the terminal, in a browser, or inside Cockpit.

title: Introduction
text: What is using this port? The owning process, the project and framework it serves, its systemd unit or Windows service, its Docker, Podman or Kubernetes container, and the user it runs as. Who can reach it? Whether the port is bound to every interface, one address or loopback only, and what the host

title: Installation
text: portop is a single static binary. Package managers keep it up to date; the release archives work anywhere.

title: Installation
text: System Command Updates Debian, Ubuntu APT repository apt upgrade Linux with snapd sudo snap install portop automatic macOS, Linux brew install portop brew upgrade Windows winget install padovanl.portop winget upgrade Windows Microsoft Store automatic

title: Installation
text: Release binaries are not notarized. If macOS blocks a binary downloaded with a browser, run portop once, open System Settings → Privacy & Security and choose Open Anyway . Homebrew and the install script are not affected.

title: First run and permissions
text: portop needs no configuration. What it can see depends on the user it runs as.

title: First run and permissions
text: portop # every listening and established socket portop 8080 # filtered on a port portop --listen # listening sockets only The table refreshes every two seconds. Press ? for help and q to quit.

title: First run and permissions
text: System Without privileges With privileges Linux Other users' sockets appear without a process; the status bar counts them, for example (3 hidden — try sudo) . sudo portop resolves every row and lets portop read the firewall. macOS lsof omits other users' sockets entirely. sudo portop lists them. Win

title: First run and permissions
text: Use a terminal with 256 colors or true color. In a minimal SSH or container session where TERM=xterm , set TERM=xterm-256color or COLORTERM=truecolor .

title: The table
text: One row per socket. Optional columns appear as the terminal gets wider; click a heading, or press s , to sort by it.

title: The table
text: Column Shows PORT Local port and its service name ( :22 ssh ), colored by exposure on listening rows. PROTO TCP or UDP ; 6 marks IPv6. STATE The TCP state. A bound, unconnected UDP socket is UNCONN and counts as listening. PROCESS The owning process; nginx +3 when three workers share the socket. PID

title: The table
text: A listening port is colored by who can reach it, at any terminal width: Color Bound to Reachable from Red 0.0.0.0 , :: Every network the host is on, unless a firewall blocks it Amber One address That interface's network (a LAN or container network) Green 127.0.0.1 , ::1 This machine only Sorting by

title: The table
text: Key Action ↑ ↓ PgUp PgDn g G Move by row or page, to the top or bottom enter Process details k Stop the process: then y for SIGTERM or f for SIGKILL o Open the port in the browser, at the bound address for single-interface listeners f , / Filter; every word must match the port, PID, process, user, u

title: The table
text: Click to select, double-click for details, right-click for the kill confirmation, middle-click to open the port, scroll with the wheel, click a heading to sort and click it again to reverse.

title: The table
text: enter shows the command line, executable, working directory, user, memory, threads, open files, start time and, for a shared socket, its workers.

title: The table
text: k records the process's start time when the confirmation opens and checks it again just before sending the signal. If the process exited and its PID was reused in the meantime, the signal is refused. On Windows both choices end the process.

title: Command line
text: Without flags portop opens the table. Every other mode prints and exits, so it fits in scripts, cron jobs and CI.

title: Command line
text: Flag Meaning portop [WORDS] Open the table filtered on the words: portop 8080 , portop nginx 443 --listen Listening sockets only: TCP LISTEN and bound UDP --json Print one snapshot as JSON and exit --wait PORT[/udp] Wait until something listens on the port ( scripting ) --free PORT[/udp] Stop whatev

title: Command line
text: portop --json --listen | jq '.[] | select(.scope == "all") | {port: .local_port, process, firewall}' Each row is an object with these fields; fields marked optional are left out when unknown. Field Type Meaning protocol string TCP or UDP local_address , local_port string, number Bind address and por

title: Command line
text: Code Meaning 0 Success; --diff found no change; --compose found every fixed port as expected 1 Error; --wait timed out; --free could not free the port 2 Invalid flags 3 --diff found changes; --compose found an unused or conflicting port

title: Scripting
text: --wait and --free handle the two port chores of development and CI: waiting for a service, and getting a port back.

title: Scripting
text: portop --wait 5432 --timeout 1m && ./migrate Exits 0 as soon as something listens on the port, or 1 when the timeout (default 30s) passes. Add /udp for a UDP port: --wait 53/udp .

title: Scripting
text: portop --free 3000 # SIGTERM, then wait up to 5s for the port portop --free 3000 --force # SIGKILL to every process holding it portop --free 53/udp --yes # no confirmation --free lists what it will stop and, on a terminal, asks for confirmation. It records each process's start time before asking and

title: Scripting
text: # ports reachable from the network portop --json --listen | jq -r '.[] | select(.scope != "loopback") | "\(.local_port)/\(.protocol) \(.process // "?")"' # who listens on 8080 portop --json --listen 8080 | jq '.[0] | {pid, process, user, container}'

title: Configuration
text: Everything is optional. Command-line flags win over the file.

title: Configuration
text: Press , in the table to preview the 13 themes live and rebind any of the 20 actions. Changes are saved to the configuration file at once.

title: Configuration
text: portop --init-config writes a commented file in the OS configuration directory: ~/.config/portop/config.yml on Linux, ~/Library/Application Support/portop/config.yml on macOS, %AppData%\portop\config.yml on Windows. --config uses another. theme: tokyo-night # default, dracula, nord, solarized, gruvb

title: Baseline drift
text: Record which ports a host is supposed to listen on, then let a timer tell you when that changes.

title: Baseline drift
text: portop --save-baseline # record what listens now portop --diff # exit 3 if anything changed portop --diff --json # the same, for scripts The baseline is a small JSON file in the OS config directory; --baseline-path chooses another.

title: Baseline drift
text: Each listening TCP and UDP port is recorded with its scope : loopback, every interface or one address. A service listening on IPv4 and IPv6 is one entry. --diff reports: ports listening now that were not in the baseline; ports in the baseline that no longer listen; ports whose scope changed, for exa

title: Baseline drift
section: Run it from a systemd timer
text: # /etc/systemd/system/portop-diff.service [Unit] Description=Compare listening ports with the baseline [Service] Type=oneshot ExecStart=/usr/bin/portop --diff --baseline-path /var/lib/portop/baseline.json # /etc/systemd/system/portop-diff.timer [Timer] OnCalendar=hourly [Install] WantedBy=timers.tar

title: Projects and frameworks
text: For every listening process, portop looks for the project it was started from and the framework serving it, so a port reads storefront · Next.js instead of node . Each row also gets a category.

title: Projects and frameworks
text: portop starts from the process's working directory, or from a script on its command line when the process runs from / (a service started as node /srv/app/server.js ), and walks up to the nearest project manifest: Manifest Language Frameworks recognised package.json Node.js Next.js, Nuxt, Astro, Remi

The filter matches project, framework and language, and a category name typed whole ( dev ) shows that categ

title: Projects and frameworks
text: On Linux portop reads /proc ; on macOS one ps and one lsof call cover every new process; on Windows the working directory is read from the process itself, which Windows allows for your own processes. Detection runs once per process and is cached while it lives.

title: Containers and workers
text: portop names the container behind a port and tells a server's master process from its workers.

title: Containers and workers
text: On Linux the container ID comes from the process's cgroup and the name from the Engine API. The socket is found the way the docker CLI finds it: a unix:// DOCKER_HOST , /var/run/docker.sock , rootless Docker in $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR , Docker Desktop's ~/.docker/run/docker.sock , then Podman's /run/podman

title: Containers and workers
text: On a node running containerd or CRI-O, a pod's process is shown as namespace/pod/container . The names come from the kubelet's log links in /var/log/containers , so no API access or crictl is needed; run portop on the node, usually with sudo .

title: Containers and workers
section: Docker Desktop on macOS and Windows
text: Containers run inside a VM, so their processes are not visible to the host. portop recognises them by the host ports Docker publishes, which labels the listening rows.

title: Containers and workers
text: Pre-forking servers such as nginx, gunicorn, php-fpm and Apache share one listening socket between a master and its workers. portop shows one row owned by the master, the process whose parent does not hold the socket, and counts the others: nginx +3 . The details list the workers' PIDs and JSON has

text: For every listening port the network can reach, portop asks the host firewall whether incoming traffic gets through.

title: Platform support
text: Every feature runs on Linux, macOS and Windows. Where the operating system does not provide something, portop leaves the field empty or shows ? instead of failing.

title: Platform support
text: Feature Linux macOS Windows Sockets and owner Yes; sudo for other users' processes Yes; sudo for other users' sockets Yes, every PID Process details Yes No thread count Working directory of your own processes; no open files Project and framework Yes Yes Your own processes Stop a process SIGTERM, SIG

title: Platform support
text: Linux on amd64, arm64, ARMv7 and ARMv6 with hardware floating point; macOS on Intel and Apple Silicon; Windows 10 1809 or later and Windows 11 on x64 and ARM64. ARMv5, soft-float armel , big-endian ARM, 32-bit x86 and 32-bit Windows are not supported. The validation report lists what has been tested

title: How it works
text: portop reads what the operating system already exposes; it installs nothing and runs no daemon.

title: How it works
text: Sockets come from /proc/net/{tcp,tcp6,udp,udp6} and are matched to processes through /proc/<pid>/fd , as ss and lsof do. systemd units and container IDs come from each process's cgroup, traffic from netlink socket diagnostics.

title: How it works
text: Sockets and owners come from the machine-readable output of lsof ; process details and CPU time from ps ; traffic from nettop .

title: How it works
text: Sockets and owning PIDs come from GetExtendedTcpTable and GetExtendedUdpTable , process details from the Win32 process APIs with limited query rights, and services from the Service Control Manager.

title: How it works
text: External tools run without a shell, with a timeout and a fixed locale. Text that other processes control (names, command lines, reverse DNS, Compose values) is cleaned of terminal escape sequences and bidirectional controls before it is drawn. A signal is only sent after re-checking the target's sta

title: Troubleshooting
text: The socket belongs to another user. Run sudo portop on Linux and macOS, or use an Administrator terminal on Windows. TIME_WAIT rows never have one: the connection is closing and no process holds it.

title: Troubleshooting
text: The firewall could not be read or decides per program. See what each system reports ; on Linux, run portop with sudo .

title: Troubleshooting
text: portop cannot reach the Docker or Podman socket. Check DOCKER_HOST , membership of the docker group, or run with sudo . On Kubernetes nodes, /var/log/containers must be readable.

title: Troubleshooting
text: The terminal reports 16 colors. Set TERM=xterm-256color or COLORTERM=truecolor .

title: Troubleshooting
text: The process exited or was replaced since the row was shown; portop refuses to signal a different process. Refresh with r and try again.

title: Troubleshooting
text: Open an issue with portop --version , the operating system and, if useful, portop --json output.
